overview: This file concerns Nichols Engineering & Research Corporation’s effort to obtain technical and operating data about flash roasters it had designed in 1940 for a Japanese sulfuric-acid installation associated with Mitsui and Toyo Koatsu Kogyo K.K. The State Department identified the probable plant as the 50,000-metric-ton-capacity facility at Sunagawa, Hokkaido, but explained that it had only begun limited operation in 1946, that the use of Nichols’s designs could not be confirmed, and that Occupation engineering personnel could not yet undertake the requested study. Fragmentary internal notes discuss the possible installation of three roasters, doubts about whether flash-roaster equipment was actually used, and possible ways to refer the inquiry to officials in Japan. A final 1948 transfer sheet records the refiling of a Nanjing telegram under a Japan-related decimal-file number, although the telegram itself is absent.

subfiles.title: Nichols Engineering request for data on Japanese flash roasters
subfiles.from: R. W. Rowen, Nichols Engineering & Research Corporation
subfiles.to: Far East Division, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Nichols requests extensive technical information about flash roasters and associated sulfuric-acid equipment believed to have been installed for Toyo Koatsu Kogyo in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rowen explains that Nichols supplied Mitsui’s New York company with designs in 1940 for four furnaces intended to roast iron pyrite in suspension and produce sulfur-dioxide gas. The letter requests operating capacities, feed analyses, preparation methods, gas strengths, calcine composition, detailed waste-heat-boiler performance, gas-cleaning arrangements, maintenance experience and installation history. Nichols also seeks assembly drawings and information about any similar installations because it is designing additional large flash-roaster plants.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on the Sunagawa sulfuric-acid plant
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.to: R. W. Rowen, Nichols Engineering & Research Corporation
subfiles.about: Whitman identifies Sunagawa as the probable site but declines to commission the requested engineering investigation while the plant remains in limited initial operation.
subfiles.summary: The State Department reports that the probable plant was at Sunagawa on Hokkaido and had not begun operating until 1946; it was still far below its stated annual capacity of 50,000 metric tons of sulfuric acid. Whitman notes that purchasing a foreign design did not prove that Japanese industry actually installed it and says available information did not confirm flash roasters at this or any other Toyo Koatsu plant. Because performance data would be premature and Occupation engineers had many other assignments, he recommends postponing the investigation until private trade and business travel resume. The copy bears a November 14 date and a drafting notation dated November 7, 1946.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum and handwritten notes on handling the Nichols inquiry
subfiles.about: Fragmentary internal notes assess available plant information and propose alternatives for referring or answering Nichols’s inquiry.
subfiles.summary: The notes mention what appears to be Herreshoff-type roasters, three installed roasters, a 50,000-metric-ton capacity and ammonium sulfate, while indicating that the plant was not operating or not near capacity in 1946. They also express uncertainty that flash equipment was installed. Gantenbein reportedly advised that “FA” handled American property interests rather than technical inquiries, after which Martin suggested either telling Nichols to write Atcheson directly or having the Department contact Atcheson and acknowledge Nichols’s request.

subfiles.title: Transfer sheet for Nanjing telegram no. 1383
subfiles.about: The sheet records the transfer of a July 29, 1948 telegram from Nanjing to another State Department decimal-file classification.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State’s Division of Communications and Records identifies the item as telegram no. 1383 from Nanjing, rendered by the OCR as “Tanking.” The underlying correspondence was dated July 29, 1948, while the transfer appears to have been recorded on September 29, 1948. The sheet links file references 894.64/7-2948 and 800.50 Japan/9-2948, but it preserves none of the telegram’s substantive content.

interest: The file illustrates how an American engineering company tried to recover operational knowledge from equipment designed before the Pacific War and potentially installed in Japan during wartime. It is especially useful for the history of industrial technology transfer because the State Department explicitly warns that the purchase of designs did not establish their actual use. The reply and internal notes also document the practical limits of technical intelligence during the early Occupation, when Japanese plants were only slowly restarting and qualified Occupation engineers had competing assignments. The 1948 transfer sheet offers a small but useful example of State Department filing practices and the movement of records between decimal classifications.
